title: Advertising trucks: seating arrangement
summary: With Kid Rene he played dance halls and advertising trucks, where the trombone sat at the tailgate, the clarinet near the cab and the bass at the rear.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: I wondered where you worked with him, which halls, when you played dance band?

Well, I played at the economy hall, and the carburetor hall, I remember playing with Kid René. And one job we had over the river, you know, we had to go to the river and play. And, uh, that was a large hall too. Yeah. Yeah, we played over there. And, um, for René playing parades, I can't swear to that that he played any, or I played any with him. But he played a lot of advertisements, I played a lot of them with him. On the, on the trucks, you know. Yeah, uh, what's it called, a tear gate. Yeah. To do, yeah, we played a lot of those.
Where'd they put the clarinet? Where did you sit on those trucks?

Well, I always had a seat on the side, you know. The trombone was always on the tear gate, and I was next to the trumpet, and it was close to the cab of the, the cab up there. The cab up there. Yes, uh, most of the time, I was right at the cab. Because, uh.
You'd be fairly close to the drum then, would you be? Uh.

Where'd they have the drum? Yeah, the drum was on the opposite side of us. Most of the time, we, the trumpet and the clarinet would be on one side, the drum would be on the other, and the banjo may be next to the drum. Uh-huh. But the trombone and bass would usually be in the rear, because a lot of times the truck had a top on it, and so the bass player, you either have to lay bass down and play it, or get to the rear of the truck, so you could hold it straight up.
